newsitem.title: INDIA: India unveils steps to strengthen state oil firms.
newsitem.headline: India unveils steps to strengthen state oil firms.

text.p: India, starved of oil to meet growing demand, on Friday gave domestic firms a level playing field in oil-sharing contracts but shied away from the bitter medicine needed to cure a mounting subsidy bill.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, unveiling the 1997/98 (April-March) federal budget, said under a new exploration licensing policy, firms including state-controlled Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd (OIL), would be paid the international price of oil for new discoveries.
The domestic firms would get the same duty concessions on imports of capital goods as private production-sharing contracts, Chidambaram added.

India's demand for petroleum products is growing at over eight percent annually, much faster than the growth in domestic supplies. Only six of 26 basins with potential for oil and gas in the country have so far been explored.
"We cannot choke this growth. At the same time, we must reduce our dependence on imported petroleum products. There is no real alternative to increasing the supply," Chidambaram said.
The Indian goverment said on Friday that crude oil production in 1997/98 (April-March) was targeted at 34.37 million tonnes compared with an estimated 33.72 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Chidambaram said that exploration companies would have the freedom to market crude oil and gas in the domestic market.
He said the government also wanted to allow refineries to import capital goods at a concessional duty during the ninth plan (1997-2002) period.
But Chidambaram did not announce any measures to cut import tariffs on crude oil and raise them for refined products or measures to stem the growing subsidy bill.
Oil analysts in Bombay recently said the government was expected to cut import tariffs for crude oil and might raise them for refined products in the 1997/98 budget.
If the differentials between crude and product tariffs were restructured, it would be a key step towards liberalising the refining industry, analysts said.

Junior Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu said earlier on Friday the government would owe state-controlled oil firms 158 billion rupees ($4.4 billion) by the end of March, up from 57 billion rupees one year earlier.
The oil companies have been pressing Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government to increase prices so as to raise the funds needed to repay the money.
The shortfall, called the oil pool deficit, is the amount the government owes oil companies for selling petroleum products to Indian consumers way below world prices.
Oil companies shoulder the burden of the deficit while they wait for the state to pay them back, but the increasing strain on their liquidity is forcing companies to borrow. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
